strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in high-fidelity salient-object segmentation: scarce, expensive pixel-level annotations and poor cross-dataset generalization.
The proposed synthetic dataset is unusually large, and the synthetic-only cross-dataset results are promising across DIS, HR-SOD, and conventional SOD benchmarks.
The paper evaluates several relevant components, including synthetic-data alternatives, generation rounds, feature modalities, decoder branches, prompt generation, and computational efficiency.
The qualitative examples and manual audit of 1,000 generated masks provide useful preliminary evidence that the generation pipeline can produce diverse, reasonably aligned image-mask pairs.
weaknesses: The central label-generation mechanism is insufficiently specified. The paper describes learned projections and a fusion network that decode masks from FLUX, concept-attention, and DINO-v3 features, but does not explain what supervision trains this decoder, which data are used, or provide its objective and training protocol. This makes the core contribution difficult to assess or reproduce.

The ambiguity claim is not convincingly validated. Training images have only one annotation, no mechanism explicitly encourages diversity among mask branches, and no multi-annotation benchmark or diversity analysis is presented. The non-oracle three-mask model improves only slightly over one mask and the two-mask model is worse; best-of-three oracle scores cannot establish ambiguity handling.

There are important methodological contradictions and quantitative errors. The best branch is variously described as minimizing IoU, using actual IoU, and using predicted IoU. The claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure improvements from iterative generation do not match Table 5, where absolute F-measure changes are approximately 0.002 and 0.005.

The dataset accounting appears inconsistent: 100 initial images for each of 1,676 reported objects/categories would already exceed the final 139,981 images, before the stated additional 50,000 images and only 6.8% filtering. The exact round sizes, category definition, and retained sample counts need reconciliation.

Comparisons do not cleanly isolate the effects of synthetic data, the DINO-v3 backbone, architecture, and training compute. Several headline comparisons use baselines with different architectures or pretrained representations, while the ablation indicates that DINO-v3 itself accounts for most of the architectural gain.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a dataset-and-training contribution of this scale: release status is unclear and key details such as generation-decoder training, student optimization, input resolutions, schedules, augmentations, per-round sampling, prompt/category construction, and filtering-model training are missing.

The quality evaluation is underdefined. FID lacks a specified real reference distribution, feature implementation, and sample count, and comparing FID across datasets with potentially different category distributions is questionable. The Inception Score also changes from 98.1 in Table 8 to 35.19 in Table 9 without explaining the evaluation subsets or protocols.

Results are reported without repeated runs, uncertainty, or significance analysis, despite several ablation gains being very small. Dataset provenance, biases inherited from FLUX/DINO/VLM models, licensing, and other ethical considerations are also not discussed.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: reducing dependence on expensive pixel-accurate annotations while improving transfer between DIS and high-resolution salient-object detection.
The proposed dataset is unusually large for this area, with 139,981 synthetic images, and the qualitative examples show considerable category, scene, and resolution diversity.

The cross-dataset evaluation spans multiple established benchmarks and reports several complementary segmentation metrics. The controlled 10,000-image comparison in Table 4 provides useful evidence that S3OD data can improve generalization more than MaskFactory or DatasetDM data under the authors' setup.
Combining diffusion features, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features is a potentially useful direction. The modality ablation indicates that the full combination generally performs best.
The paper is reasonably organized and includes useful qualitative results, efficiency measurements, prompting details, and a small manual dataset-quality assessment.
weaknesses: The central data-generation method is not reproducible. The manuscript never adequately explains how the mask-producing fusion network/DPT decoder is trained, including the source of its supervisory masks, training datasets, objective, split, and optimization details. Without this information, it is impossible to determine whether the method truly eliminates a teacher bottleneck or whether evaluation data could influence mask generation.

The iterative-generation protocol is critically underspecified. The paper says category weights are derived from performance on a held-out test set, but does not identify that set, explain how its categories are annotated, or establish that benchmark test images are excluded. This leaves a serious potential test-leakage concern.

The main comparisons conflate data, architecture, and pretrained-backbone effects. Table 7 shows that switching from Swin-B to DINO-v3 produces a much larger gain than adding multiple masks, yet there is no controlled comparison against baselines retrained with the same DINO-v3 backbone, optimization, input resolution, and amount of data.

The evidence does not support the claimed ambiguity contribution. Only one annotation is available per image, so the model cannot learn distinct valid interpretations directly. Best-of-three oracle evaluation uses ground truth at test time and will improve mechanically with multiple candidates; it neither measures real ambiguity nor demonstrates useful inference-time selection. The deployable, predicted-IoU result is only modestly better than the one-mask variant, while two masks are worse.

Several quantitative claims appear incorrect. For example, Table 5 changes DIS F-measure from 0.879 to 0.881 and DUT-OMRON from 0.855 to 0.860, not the claimed 3.6% and 5.3% gains. The paper also inconsistently reports prompt-based Inception Scores of 98.1 in Table 8 and 35.19 in Table 9 without explaining the protocols.

The dataset accounting is unclear or internally inconsistent. An initial round of 100 images per category, followed by two additional rounds totaling at least 100,000 images, is difficult to reconcile with the final 139,981 images and the reported 1,676 unique objects. It is also unclear whether 139,981 is measured before or after the stated 6.8% filtering.

Dataset-quality evidence is weak. The FID values omit the real reference distribution, sample count, preprocessing, and feature implementation, making the unusually low scores uninterpretable. The 1,000-mask audit lacks a documented sampling protocol, independent annotators, agreement statistics, and evaluation of subtle boundary errors.

Important implementation details are missing, including training resolution, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, epochs, batch size, augmentations, prompt/category construction, category counts, mask-decoder training, and complete filtering prompts. No concrete code, model, or dataset release mechanism is given, despite the contribution depending on substantial compute and proprietary or externally hosted models.

The written formulation contains technical inconsistencies: the displayed focal loss includes only the positive-class term rather than the standard binary focal loss, and the architecture caption says loss is propagated through the branch with the highest predicted IoU whereas the method text defines assignment using actual IoU to ground truth.

The work does not discuss synthetic-data biases, licensing and redistribution constraints, contamination from large pretrained models, environmental cost of generating roughly 140,000 high-resolution samples with a 12B-parameter model, or limitations of VLM-based filtering. Overall, the promising empirical results are insufficiently controlled and documented to substantiate the paper's central claims at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving cross-domain generalization in salient-object segmentation while reducing dependence on costly pixel-level annotations.

S3OD is ambitious in scale, with 139,981 synthetic images, an adaptive category-sampling loop, and a multimodal labeling pipeline combining diffusion, concept-attention, and DINO-v3 features. The manuscript is clearly presented and visually polished. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/c7e6e569e972456b945e6392075c6cb7/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The cross-dataset evaluation is broader and more informative than standard within-benchmark testing. Synthetic-only training produces impressive results, while fine-tuning is competitive across DIS and HR-SOD benchmarks.
The controlled comparison in Table 4 provides useful evidence that S3OD data generalizes better than similarly sized MaskFactory and DatasetDM subsets on several out-of-domain datasets.
The paper includes ablations of feature modalities, generation rounds, prompts, backbones, and mask branches, as well as a manual audit of 1,000 generated annotations and an efficiency comparison.
weaknesses: The central mask-generation procedure is insufficiently specified. The paper introduces a learned fusion/decoding module but does not clearly state which labeled data train it, the objective and optimization protocol, or how splits avoid benchmark leakage. This omission makes the principal dataset contribution difficult to reproduce and weakens the claim that the method eliminates teacher bottlenecks.

The iterative generation protocol is ambiguous about the "held-out test set" used for category-wise feedback and about the exact definition of the transformation-based IoU score. If benchmark test data influence sampling, the reported cross-dataset results would be contaminated; the paper must explicitly identify this set and establish separation from all evaluation data.

Several gains are confounded by backbone and scale. Table 7 attributes a much larger improvement to replacing Swin-B with DINO-v3 than to using three masks, while principal baseline models use older representations. Data comparisons are limited to 10,000-sample subsets and lack scale-matched curves, multiple training seeds, confidence intervals, and stronger controls using the same backbone and training recipe.

The ambiguity claim is not convincingly validated. Training uses only one annotation per image, offers no explicit diversity objective, and may allow the mask branches to collapse. Best-of-three oracle evaluation cannot establish genuine ambiguity because it also rewards ordinary ensemble variation. Multi-annotator data, pairwise diversity analyses, branch-usage statistics, calibration of the IoU selector, and comparisons with ensembles or probabilistic segmentation methods are needed.

There are consequential technical inconsistencies: Section 3 defines the supposedly best branch using argmin IoU, which selects the worst-overlap mask; Figure 2 instead says assignment uses the highest predicted IoU, whereas the text otherwise suggests ground-truth IoU. The displayed focal-loss equation also omits the negative-class term. These issues leave the implemented training objective unclear.

Some quantitative claims are unreliable or under-specified. From one to three rounds, Table 5 changes F-measure from .879 to .881 on DIS and .855 to .860 on DUT-OMRON, not the stated 3.6% and 5.3% gains. Inception Score is 98.1 in Table 8 but 35.19 for S3OD in Table 9 without explaining different protocols, and the FID reference distribution, sample count, and preprocessing are not stated.

Reproducibility and responsible-release information is limited: there is no clear commitment or link for releasing the 139K-image dataset, masks, code, checkpoints, category list, filtering prompts, or generation metadata. Computational cost is given only for downstream training, and potential biases, licensing constraints, and harmful synthetic content are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents an unusually large synthetic SOD dataset, a multimodal annotation pipeline, iterative sampling, and a multi-mask architecture in one coherent framework.

The empirical scope is broad: six SOD/DIS benchmarks, cross-dataset evaluation, retraining of BiRefNet and MVANet, comparisons with other synthetic-data methods, transfer to camouflaged-object detection, efficiency measurements, and several ablations.

The reported downstream improvements are often substantial, especially for cross-domain evaluation and synthetic-only downstream training. Retraining competing architectures on S3OD usefully suggests that some gains come from the dataset rather than only the proposed network.

The manuscript is generally well organized and includes informative qualitative examples, feature visualizations, dataset-quality analysis, and limitations. weaknesses: The central characterization as learning from synthetic data without teacher bottlenecks is misleading. The mask decoder used to annotate S3OD is explicitly supervised on DIS-5K, HRSOD, UHRSD, and DUTS, while DINO-v3 is also pretrained on large-scale real data. Thus, the supposed synthetic-only model indirectly distills real labeled data from essentially all evaluated domains. This seriously weakens the claimed cross-dataset and zero-real-data conclusions and makes comparisons against models trained on only one real dataset difficult to interpret.

The dataset accounting is internally inconsistent. The paper reports 1,676 categories and 100 first-round images per category, implying 167,600 initial images; it then adds 25,000 images in each of two later rounds. Even after filtering 6.8%, this would yield roughly 202,800 images, not the reported 139,981. This affects reproducibility and confidence in the iterative-generation experiments.

The iterative-generation ablation is confounded by dataset size: later rounds add more training samples, but there is no equally sized randomly sampled control. Moreover, the category difficulty score is augmentation consistency rather than accuracy, so it may prioritize equivariance failures instead of weak semantic categories. The stated 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure gains also do not match Table 7, where F-measure changes are only 0.002 and 0.005.

The ambiguity claim is not convincingly validated. Training and evaluation use one annotation per image, and an oracle best-of-three result can reflect ordinary ensemble coverage rather than genuine alternative interpretations. There is no multi-annotator benchmark, ambiguity-stratified analysis, or evaluation of the predicted-IoU selector. Two masks perform worse than one, while three provide only a small gain.

Several technical definitions are erroneous or unclear. The best branch is written as argmin IoU although it should be argmax; the displayed focal loss contains only a positive-class term and omits the usual background contribution; and the text alternates between selecting by actual and predicted IoU. These issues prevent a precise assessment or reproduction of the method.

The modality ablation does not include key single-modality configurations such as DINO-v3 alone, and the incremental benefits of DiT and concept maps are often tiny or inconsistent across metrics. No multiple-run variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported. Filtering stages likewise lack ablations.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a dataset-scale contribution: essential optimizer, schedule, batch size, resolution, epoch, augmentation, decoder-training, sampling, and metric-protocol details are missing, and no concrete code/data release commitment is provided. The very low FID values and differing Inception Scores are not supported by enough protocol detail. Licensing, bias, content-safety, and environmental implications of generating and releasing roughly 140,000 FLUX images are also not adequately discussed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: the scarcity of precise, high-resolution annotations for salient-object and dichotomous segmentation.
The proposed synthetic dataset is unusually large, and the experiments cover numerous SOD, DIS, and camouflaged-object benchmarks with several established metrics.
Synthetic-data training produces substantial cross-dataset improvements, and retraining BiRefNet and MVANet on S3OD provides useful evidence that some gains transfer beyond the proposed architecture.
The modality, synthetic-baseline, architecture, and loss ablations are directionally informative, while the qualitative examples generally show plausible images and masks.
weaknesses: The central "synthetic-only" interpretation is seriously confounded. The decoder that creates the synthetic masks is itself supervised using DIS-5K, HR-SOD, UHRSOD, and DUTS annotations. Thus, real benchmark supervision enters the label-generation pipeline, making this closer to teacher-mediated knowledge expansion than learning solely from synthetic supervision. The paper neither analyzes this dependency nor clearly specifies the train/test splits used at this stage.

The iterative-generation experiment does not isolate the claimed feedback mechanism: later rounds also contain more data, and there is no equal-size control using uniform or random category sampling. Moreover, the held-out set used to update category weights is insufficiently specified, creating a risk of benchmark-adaptive generation. The claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure gains also do not match the changes reported in Table 7.

Evidence for ambiguity-aware prediction is weak. Every training image has only one annotation, branches are initially pushed toward that same annotation, and no multiply annotated or human-evaluated ambiguous benchmark is used. Oracle best-mask evaluation uses ground truth at inference and only shows that one prediction may be closer to the label, not that alternatives are semantically valid. The deployable selected-mask advantage is small and lacks uncertainty estimates.

The method description contains consequential inconsistencies: the best branch is written repeatedly as arg min IoU although it should be arg max; the figure caption describes selection using predicted IoU while the text uses actual IoU; and the stated focal-loss equation omits the background term of standard binary focal loss.

Key ablations are missing. There is no controlled scaling curve, no comparison of equally sized static versus iterative S3OD, no label-generator baseline using only DINO or a conventional teacher under matched capacity, and no experiment quantifying how much real labeled data is required to train the synthetic-mask decoder.

Reported dataset-quality evidence is inadequately documented. Extremely low FID values are presented without the reference set, sample count, preprocessing, or uncertainty. Manual inspection covers only 1,000 of roughly 140,000 samples and lacks annotator counts, agreement, sampling details, or evaluation criteria. UMAP plots do not establish distributional coverage.

Results are presented as single numbers without multiple seeds, variance, or significance testing, despite several claimed improvements being only a few thousandths. Some conclusions, such as benchmark saturation or overfitting by competing methods, are asserted without direct supporting experiments.

Reproducibility is poor for a contribution centered on a large generation pipeline: optimizer and scheduling details, input resolutions, augmentations, splits, precise generation configuration, filtering prompts, category assignments, and release commitments are missing. Reproducing the work also requires substantial compute and several large pretrained or externally aligned models.

The architecture is characterized as lightweight or streamlined, but it has approximately 117M parameters, requires 0.807 TFLOPs, and runs slower than MVANet in the reported table. Broader-impact discussion also omits potential generative-model biases, licensing concerns, and downstream failure modes. strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in high-fidelity salient-object segmentation: scarce, expensive pixel-accurate annotations and weak cross-dataset generalization.

S3OD is ambitious in scale, with 139,981 high-resolution synthetic image-mask pairs spanning 1,676 categories, a multimodal labeling pipeline, iterative category sampling, and several quality-filtering stages.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad. It includes synthetic-only transfer, DIS and HR-SOD fine-tuning, six principal benchmarks, camouflaged-object detection, alternative synthetic-data methods, and comparisons with strong recent systems.
Retraining BiRefNet and MVANet on S3OD is a valuable control: improvements across architectures provide evidence that the dataset contributes beyond the proposed model.
The synthetic-only cross-dataset results are compelling, and the COD experiments suggest that the learned representation transfers beyond the exact training task.

The paper includes useful ablations of feature modalities, generation rounds, backbone, decoder branches, branch regularization, prompt generation, dataset quality, and computational efficiency. The presentation and qualitative figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The claimed synthetic-only advantage is partly confounded by substantial real-data supervision. The synthetic mask decoder is trained using DIS-5K, HRSOD, UHRSD, and DUTS, while DINO-v3 is used in both label generation and the downstream model. Thus, S3OD is not independent of the real datasets on which it is evaluated, and the paper does not isolate how much performance comes from transferred real-label supervision, the foundation backbone, or genuinely new synthetic coverage.

The ambiguity-aware contribution is not convincingly validated. Training provides only one annotation per image, early regularization pushes every branch toward that same mask, and there is no multi-annotation benchmark or human evaluation demonstrating that alternative predictions are valid interpretations. Oracle best-of-three evaluation uses ground truth at test time and cannot establish practical value. The selected-mask improvement over a single branch is small, while the two-branch model is worse.

Several central technical descriptions are inconsistent or apparently erroneous. The best branch is defined as argmin IoU even though higher IoU is better; Figure 2 instead says selection uses predicted IoU, whereas the text describes actual IoU. The displayed focal loss includes only the positive-class term, despite being presented as a binary foreground-background loss. These issues make the implemented objective difficult to verify.

The iterative-generation evaluation set is underspecified. The paper refers to a held-out test set used to update category weights but does not clearly state its source, construction, or separation from reported benchmarks. This should be explicit to rule out benchmark-directed test leakage.

Some numerical interpretations are inaccurate. From one to three rounds, Table 7 changes F-measure from .879 to .881 on DIS and .855 to .860 on DUT-OMRON, not the claimed 3.6% and 5.3% F-measure gains. Similar reliance on relative error reductions occasionally makes modest absolute changes sound larger.

Dataset-quality evaluation lacks important methodological details. The FID values are exceptionally low, but the reference distribution, sample counts, preprocessing, and feature extractor are not specified. DINO-v3-based domain-gap measurements may also favor a pipeline and downstream model that themselves use DINO-v3.

Reproducibility is limited for a contribution centered on a large dataset: there is no clear release commitment or access description, and key training details such as optimizer, schedules, augmentations, input resolution, and exact sampling/evaluation protocols are incomplete. Reproducing generation also requires substantial closed or rapidly evolving foundation-model infrastructure and high compute.

Overall, the results are promising enough to be near the acceptance boundary, but the real-supervision confound, weak evidence for the ambiguity claim, objective inconsistencies, and incomplete protocol specification prevent the main claims from being sufficiently controlled for acceptance in their current form.
